rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links 3:187 to 3:183–184: Muhammad's advent was predicted in both Testaments, whose followers were charged to spread the prophecy rather than suppress it.
rows.anchor: to spread this prophecy and not - as they actually have done - to suppress it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses the bargain as illusory immunity in the afterlife: Jews rely on chosen status, while Christians rely on Jesus' vicarious atonement.
rows.anchor: the belief of the Jews that they are "God's chosen people", and to the conviction of the Christians that their belief in Jesus' "vicarious atonement"

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi says the people have not preserved the integrity of the Bible or Abraham's faith, despite their claims.
rows.anchor: have not, in spite of all their claims, preserved the integrity of the Bible and of Abraham's faith (Razi)

rows.speaker: the classical commentators
rows.claim: Most classical commentators choose nafs as 'human being' and assume it refers here to Adam.
rows.anchor: most of the classical commentators choose "human being", and assume that it refers here to Adam

rows.speaker: Muhammad 'Abduh
rows.claim: Abduh rejects the Adam reading and prefers 'humankind' because it stresses common origin and human brotherhood without binding the verse to the Biblical creation story.
rows.anchor: Muhammad 'Abduh, however, rejects this interpretation (Manar IV, 323 ff.) and gives, instead, his preference to "humankind"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders nafs as 'living entity', following Abduh's reasoning about humanity's common origin.
rows.anchor: My rendering of nafs, in this context, as "living entity" follows the same reasoning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zawj can denote either member of an animate pair; for humans it means either a woman's husband or a man's wife.
rows.anchor: with reference to human beings, it signifies a woman's mate (husband) as well as a man's mate (wife).

rows.speaker: Abu Muslim
rows.claim: Abu Muslim interprets minha as 'from its own kind', meaning each sex's counterpart is created from the same kind; this supports Abduh's reading.
rows.anchor: Abu Muslim - as quoted by Razi - interprets the phrase "He created out of it (minha) its mate" as meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says the literal 'out of it' points to the biological fact that both sexes originated from one living entity.
rows.anchor: the biological fact that both sexes have originated from "one living entity".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad explains the hypothetical commands as God-inspired commands issued through the Prophet.
rows.anchor: by means of the God-inspired commands issued by the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun refers to the half-hearted, who are unready for the sacrifices their faith demands.
rows.anchor: the pronoun obviously relates to the half-hearted, who are not prepared to undergo the sacrifices which their faith demands of them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call to risk life for faith and freedom or leave one's homeland introduces the long discussion of fighting in God's cause from verse 71.
rows.anchor: introduces, as it were, the long passage beginning with verse 71, which deals with fighting in God's cause.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses the phrase as 'cause them to enter into'.
rows.anchor: cause them to enter into

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad places this among the Qur'an's last revealed sections, dating it by consensus to the Farewell Pilgrimage in 10 AH; the surah title comes from the disciples' request and Jesus' prayer.
rows.anchor: the consensus of opinion places it in the period of his Farewell Pilgrimage, in the year 10 H.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah opens with believers' spiritual and social responsibilities and closes by stressing humanity's dependence on God.
rows.anchor: The surah begins with a call to the believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says the surah warns against expanding divine ordinances through subjective deduction, which burdens practice and may lead people to deny revelation itself.
rows.anchor: not to enlarge the area of divine ordinances by means of subjective

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning against taking Jews and Christians as allies means avoiding their way of life and social concepts when these conflict with Islam's principles.
rows.anchor: not to take the Jews and the Christians for their "allies" in the moral sense of the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says Jews and Christians abandoned and corrupted their prophets' truths; he singles out Jewish spiritual blindness and deafness and Christian deification of Jesus against Jesus' own teaching.
rows.anchor: both the Jews and the Christians have abandoned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an recognizes a distinct law and way of life for each religious community and calls them to compete in good works.
rows.anchor: Unto every one of you have We appointed a [different] law and way of life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True believers of whatever persuasion who believe in God and the Last Day and do righteous deeds are assured they need not fear or grieve.
rows.anchor: all who believe in God and the Last Day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad calls verse 3 the surah's crowning statement: shortly before the Prophet's death, God perfected the religious law, completed His blessing, and made self-surrender to Him the religion.
rows.anchor: the full measure of My blessings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The offerings are pilgrimage animals brought to Mecca for sacrifice in God's name, with most meat distributed to the poor.
rows.anchor: to be sacrificed there in the name of God and most of their flesh distributed among the poor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Garlands identify these animals and keep them from inadvertent profane or commercial use.
rows.anchor: to prevent their being inadvertently used for profane (e.g., commercial) ends, garlands are customarily hung around their necks.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sha'a'ir Allah includes places for rites such as the Ka'bah and the rites themselves; in context it refers especially to pilgrimage rites.
rows.anchor: denotes the places reserved for particular religious rites (e.g., the Ka'bah) as well as the religious rites themselves.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses idha halaltum as becoming free of the obligations attached to pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: when you have become free of the obligations attaching to the state of pilgrimage

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators read the injunction as referring to the events culminating in the Hudaybiyyah truce.
rows.anchor: the view of some of the commentators that the above verse alludes to the events culminating in the truce of Hudaybiyyah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad rejects that historical restriction because the surah dates to 10 AH, after Muslims held Mecca and nearly all Quraysh had embraced Islam.
rows.anchor: At the time of the revelation of this surah Mecca was already in the possession of the Muslims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The injunction therefore has timeless scope: it covers anyone who physically or metaphorically blocks believers from religious duties and so leads them away from faith.
rows.anchor: that it refers to anybody who might endeavour to bar the believers - physically or metaphorically - from the exercise of their religious duties

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forbidden things are not among the good things of life, while anything not expressly forbidden is allowed.
rows.anchor: what has been forbidden does not belong to the category of "the good things of life" (at-tayyibat)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says the Qur'an forbids only things or actions injurious physically, morally, or socially.
rows.anchor: the Qur'an forbids only those things or actions which are injurious to man physically, morally or socially.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mukallib means trained like a hunting dog and applies to any trained hunting animal, including a hound, falcon, or cheetah.
rows.anchor: The term mukailib signifies "trained like a [hunting) dog", and is applied to every animal used for hunting

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Many commentators understand the reference to apes and swine literally.
rows.anchor: Contrary to many of the commentators who take this reference to "apes and swine" in a literal sense

rows.speaker: Mujahid
rows.claim: Asad favors Mujahid's metaphor for sinners' moral degradation: they become unpredictable like apes and abandoned to lust like swine; Tabari also quotes this reading on 2:65.
rows.anchor: Mujahid explains it as a metaphorical description (mathal) of the moral degradation which such sinners undergo

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sinners worse than the mockers are hypocrites, especially Bible-following hypocrites, who have no excuse after revelation; the references include both Jews and Christians.
rows.anchor: the sinners who are even worse than the mockers are the hypocrites, and particularly those among them who claim to be followers of the Bible

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads intentional killing as an isolated or first offense, not persistent transgression condemned in the preceding verse.
rows.anchor: by the "intentional" killing referred to here only an isolated incident (or a first offence) can be meant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here game means edible animals; several authentic Traditions permit killing dangerous or highly obnoxious animals, such as snakes, scorpions, or rabid dogs, during pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: the term "game" (sayd) relates in this context only to edible animals

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The compensation offering is for distribution among the poor.
rows.anchor: for distribution among the poor.

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi reads the Ka'bah metonymically as Mecca's sacred precincts, not only the sanctuary itself.
rows.anchor: In this context, the Ka'bah signifies, metonymically, the sacred precincts of Mecca, and not only the sanctuary itself (Razi).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two upright people estimate the killed animal's flesh value and choose a domestic animal of equivalent value for compensation.
rows.anchor: The "two persons of probity" are supposed to determine the approximate flesh-value of the wild animal which has been killed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A pilgrim too poor to provide equivalent cattle may instead feed the needy or fast; someone unable to feed others may choose the fasting alternative.
rows.anchor: These two alternatives are open to a pilgrim who is too poor to provide a head or heads of cattle corresponding in value to the game which he has killed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because revelation and authentic Tradition set no number of people to feed or fasting days, Asad leaves those details to personal conscience.
rows.anchor: these details are obviously left to the conscience of the person concerned.
